equity factor.def: A trait by which stocks can be ranked, such as profitability or past return, where the ranking has predicted returns. Its return is measured as that of the top-ranked stocks minus that of the bottom-ranked ones.

long-short portfolio.def: A portfolio that buys one group of assets and sells short an equal dollar amount of another. Its return is the difference between the two groups' returns, which depends little on the market's direction.

return on equity.def: A company's profit for a year divided by the shareholders' stake in it, its book equity. Abbreviated ROE.

price-to-earnings ratio.def: A share's price divided by the company's earnings per share: how many years of current earnings the price pays for. Abbreviated P/E.

free cash flow.def: The cash a company's operations generate after the spending needed to maintain and expand its assets. Abbreviated FCF.

expense ratio.def: A fund's yearly charge as a percentage of the money invested in it, taken out of the fund's returns.

turnover.def: How much of a portfolio is sold and replaced over a year, as a share of its value. High turnover raises trading costs and, in a taxable account, realizes gains sooner.

book-to-market ratio.def: The book value of a company's equity, from its accounts, divided by its market value. A high ratio marks a stock the market prices cheaply. Abbreviated B/M.

valuation spread.def: How many times more expensive the most expensive stocks are than the cheapest, measured against book value or another fundamental. When it widens, value stocks fall behind even if their businesses do well.

capital asset pricing model.def: The textbook model in which a stock's expected return above the risk-free rate equals its beta times the market's expected return above that rate. Abbreviated CAPM.

factor timing.def: Shifting weight between equity factors according to a forecast of which will do best next, rather than holding them at fixed weights.

Federal Open Market Committee.def: The committee of the Federal Reserve that sets US short-term interest rates. It meets about eight times a year, roughly every six weeks. Abbreviated FOMC.

Fed put.def: The market's belief that the Federal Reserve will respond to a sharp fall in stocks by easing policy, which limits the losses investors expect.

rebalancing.def: Trading a portfolio back to its target weights after market moves have pushed it away from them, such as selling stocks and buying bonds when stocks have grown past their share.

front-running.def: Trading ahead of a flow you expect, so that you hold the position before the flow moves the price. In this book it means anticipating predictable public flows, such as mandated rebalancing, not the illegal use of a client's orders.

10-year Treasury note future.def: A futures contract on US government notes with about ten years to maturity, traded under the ticker ZN. Its price rises when longer-term interest rates fall.

Halloween effect.def: The pattern in which stocks have earned more from November to April than from May to October, also known as sell in May and go away. No clean mechanism for it has been found.

turn-of-the-month effect.def: The pattern of modestly higher average stock returns in the first four or five trading days of each month, attributed to pension contributions and retirement deposits being invested.

TED spread.def: The gap between the rate at which banks lend to one another for three months and the three-month Treasury bill rate: originally LIBOR minus the bill rate, now read with SOFR. It widens when banks grow reluctant to lend.

pre-FOMC drift.def: The tendency of US stocks to rise in the 24 hours before a scheduled Federal Open Market Committee announcement, documented from 1994 to 2011. It has been close to zero since 2015.

forward guidance.def: A central bank's public statements about the likely future path of its policy, meant to shape expectations between its meetings.

S&P 500 inclusion effect.def: The rise in a stock's price between the announcement that it will join the S&P 500 and its addition, when index funds must buy it. It has shrunk from about 7% in the 1990s to under 1%.
